title: Standards give scope, not sequence
statement: Standards bound what a course covers but not its order, so design the knowledge curriculum and its progression first and use standards to check coverage afterwards.
detail: The curriculum rules a second-round review applied to the reading course say standards constrain scope but do not provide a teachable sequence, and that a course needs an explicit progression spine, entry assumptions, prerequisite policy, source ladder and evidence model. A review of the course's knowledge graph found some cross-unit links matching surface knowledge when the important connection was deeper and thematic, and asked for links about big ideas instead. Each unit states one key understanding.
against: The doctrine is the project's own synthesis, not external evidence, and it inverts the standards-first build order most of the field assumes (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/skills/reading-science/applied/teaching-comprehension-insights-brainlift.qmd`). an open-questions note asked whether a sequenced knowledge spine was actually wanted, or whether units were meant to stay relatively unrelated (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0097-incept-reading-explorers-g3-open-questions-2026-07-09.qmd`). It rests on one review's request, not on a measured outcome.

evidence.quote: - Standards constrain scope but do not provide a teachable sequence.
- A course needs an explicit progression spine, entry assumptions, prerequisite policy, source ladder, and evidence model.
Make cross-unit links about big ideas rather than surface facts.
Some links appear to match surface knowledge, such as gods' names across traditions, when the important connection is deeper and thematic.
use the standard to constrain scope (what must appear), but apply independent judgement about order, depth, prerequisite structure, and cognitive demand.
standards alignment is a *check run afterward*
Skills-only reading standards ("determine the central idea") are architecturally unusable: they carry no content, no sequence, no prerequisites
Therefore the knowledge curriculum — domains, throughlines, text sets — is the load-bearing design object, and standards alignment is a *check run afterward*.
standards mislead as teaching plans — assessments are the evidence authority;
Our own synthesis (paraphrase-level cites), NOT external evidence — not quote-gated.
Add a key understanding at the top of every unit: one plain-language sentence stating what the whole unit is really about.
State standards are scope documents written for accountability and comparability, not for novice learnability.
Skills-only reading standards ("determine the central idea") are architecturally unusable: they carry no content, no sequence, no prerequisites
Reading standards are skills, not knowledge — CASE-tag coverage is plumbing, never the curriculum claim.
unit-level key understandings, conceptual rather than surface graph links
The course therefore treats official topic IDs as scope constraints, not as a ready-made lesson order.
